title: Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium Guideline (CPIC) for CYP2D6, ADRB1, ADRB2, ADRA2C, GRK4, and GRK5 genotypes and beta-blocker therapy
authors: Duarte JD, Thomas CD, Lee CR, Huddart R, Agundez JAG, Baye JF, et al.
funder: This work was funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for CPIC (R24GM115264 and U24HG010135) and PharmGKB (U24HG010615). Additional grant funding includes R01HG011800, K08HL146990, the Robert Bosch Stiftung Stuttgart, R35 GM131770, P50MD017351 and R01HL132154.
authorConflicts: One author directs PharmVar and consults for Delix Pharmaceuticals; one consults for Janssen, Ortho Diagnostics, Cytokinetics, AstraZeneca, Otsuka, Abbott Laboratories and Illumina, has participated in research funded by Amgen, Lilly, AstraZeneca, Pfizer, Bayer, Illumina and Janssen, and holds, through Henry Ford Health, a patent for a beta-blocker response polygenic score; one consults for Ariel Precision Medicine; all other authors declare no competing interests.
result: The level of evidence was graded high for associations between CYP2D6 genetic variation and both metoprolol exposure and heart-rate response, and insufficient for CYP2D6 with other beta-blockers and for any beta-blocker with ADRB1, ADRB2, ADRA2C, GRK4 or GRK5 (CPIC level C, no recommendation). Compared with normal metabolisers given the same dose, CYP2D6 poor metabolisers experience a more than twofold longer elimination half-life and a nearly fivefold higher area under the plasma concentration-time curve of metoprolol, with greater reductions of blood pressure, approximately 3 to 6 mm Hg systolic and 2 to 6 mm Hg diastolic, and of heart rate, approximately 3 to 8 beats per minute; the effect on clinical outcomes is unclear and few well-powered studies have assessed the risk of bradycardia. Recommendations for metoprolol: normal metabolisers, initiate standard dosing (strong); intermediate metabolisers, initiate standard dosing (moderate), since increased concentrations do not appear to translate into clinically significant changes; poor metabolisers, initiate therapy with the lowest recommended starting dose, titrate carefully to clinical effect or the guideline-recommended dose and monitor more closely for bradycardia, or alternatively consider another beta-blocker (moderate); ultra-rapid and indeterminate phenotypes, no recommendation. No recommendation should prevent or impede up-titration to maximally tolerated or guideline-recommended doses, as in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and after myocardial infarction, and modifying therapy solely on genotype in a poor metaboliser already tolerating a stable regimen is probably unnecessary. Beta-blockers show a sigmoid dose-response relationship, so concentrations above a threshold do not increase response further. Carvedilol, nebivolol and propranolol are also CYP2D6 substrates and poor metabolisers reach several-fold higher carvedilol and nebivolol concentrations, but published evidence of a difference in clinical response was judged insufficient. As many as 30% of patients take a concomitant CYP2D6 inhibitor, and a CYP2D6 activity score of zero should be assumed with a strong inhibitor and halved with a moderate inhibitor.
